cards.front: What should you know about stopping distance?
cards.back: The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle stops. Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

cards.front: What should you know about thinking distance?
cards.back: The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time (the time between seeing the hazard and pressing the brake).

cards.front: What should you know about braking distance?
cards.back: The distance the vehicle travels while the brakes are applied, from pressing the brake to coming to a complete stop.

cards.front: What should you know about reaction time?
cards.back: The time between seeing a hazard and responding (pressing the brake). Typical reaction time is about 0.5 seconds.

cards.front: Both thinking distance and braking distance increase with speed, but braking distance increases much more dramatically.
cards.back: If speed doubles, thinking distance doubles, but braking distance increases by a factor of 4 (it is proportional to speed²).

cards.front: What should you know about why braking distance increases with the square of speed?
cards.back: The kinetic energy of the vehicle is KE = ½mv². If speed doubles, KE quadruples. The brakes must remove all this energy, so the braking distance is proportional to v².

cards.front: Recall a key point about Stopping Distances
cards.back: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Braking distance relates to KE: F × d = ½mv², so d = ½mv²/F. If speed doubles, KE quadruples, so braking distance quadruples (d ∝ v²). You may also use t = √(2h/g) to calculate reaction time from ruler drop distance.

cards.front: What should you know about answers?
cards.back: (a) At each speed, thinking distance / speed = 6/20 = 9/30 = 12/40 = 15/50 = 18/60 = 21/70 = 0.3 m per mph. This constant ratio shows proportionality. Reaction time = 0.3 m/mph ÷ 0.447 m/s per mph ≈ 0.67 s . (b) Thinking distance ∝ speed (linear), but braking distance ∝ speed² (quadratic). KE = ½mv², so doubling speed quadruples KE and therefore quadruples the work the brakes must do. (c) At 30 mph on a dry road, total stopping distance = 23 m, so the car would just stop in time.
